sections.html:
Lyon County covers 2,024 square miles of western Nevada. Yerington is the county seat, and the communities include Fernley, Dayton, Silver Springs, Stagecoach, Smith Valley and Mound House, which sits on US 50 at the Carson City line. The 2020 count was 59,235 residents, and 74.7% of occupied homes were owner-occupied. About 7.0% of the 24,401 housing units stood vacant.

Residents are split between town and country, with 55.4% living in urban areas and 44.6% in rural ones. For a seller that means a mix of subdivision homes, ranch parcels and raw land, each with its own buyer pool and its own paperwork.

Three bodies divide the work. The Assessor values property. The Clerk-Treasurer bills and collects. The Nevada Tax Commission sets the rate each spring, working from budgets that local entities submit.

  • Assessor: 775-463-6520
  • Clerk-Treasurer: 27 S Main Street, Yerington, 775-463-6501
  • Recorder: 775-463-6581

The Assessor's job is to find taxable property, appraise it, and calculate 35% of the appraised amount as assessed value. The office sets no rate and collects nothing. Land is appraised at market value for its use. Buildings are priced at replacement cost new, then depreciated 1.5% per year to a maximum of 75%.

Market value has very little bearing on taxable value, especially as improvements age. Values can change every year, either through reappraisal or through factors the Tax Commission approves. Owners whose value changed get assessment notices in December and June.

sections.h2: When is the tax due, and how do you pay it?
sections.html:
The bill comes once a year and is paid in four installments under NRS 361.483.

InstallmentDue date
FirstThird Monday of August
SecondFirst Monday of October
ThirdFirst Monday of January
FourthFirst Monday of March

A few practical points before a sale:

  • Bills are mailed in mid to late July, since the fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30.
  • The county sends one bill to the address on file, or to the servicer when it has been told a servicer pays.
  • No bill goes out at each installment, and there are no reminders or payment confirmations.
  • A bill that never arrived does not excuse late payment. If it has not come by early August, call for a reprint.
  • A 10-day grace period follows each due date.

Payment options are online (scan the QR code on the bill or search the parcel on the county portal), by phone, in person at 27 S Main Street, by check in the drop box (no cash), or by mail to the Lyon County Treasurer. Penalties follow state law, from 4% for one late installment up to 7% for four.

Talk to the Assessor first, then file with the County Board of Equalization by January 15. When that date lands on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.

The order of appeal looks like this:

  1. Call or visit the Assessor's Office to discuss the value with an appraiser.
  2. File the appeal with the Assessor's Office by January 15.
  3. If you remain unsatisfied, appeal to the State Board of Equalization.
  4. After that, the court system.

Any of these bodies can adjust the assessed value, though none can touch a tax rate. The County Board has heard appeals in February, and its agendas list each one. Bring comparable sales, repair estimates and photos of any condition that lowers the home's worth.

sections.h2: What the Recorder requires when a house sells
sections.html:
Every transfer of title needs a Declaration of Value form so the Recorder can decide whether transfer tax is due or an exemption applies. The form accompanies deeds, contracts of sale and some court orders. Copies of a recorded deed can be requested online, by phone or in person with advance payment.

Nevada's statewide Real Property Transfer Tax is $1.95 per $500 of value, with extra amounts only in Washoe, Churchill and Clark counties. Lyon County has no add-on. Both buyer and seller are liable, and the tax is collected when the deed is recorded. Exemptions include transfers to or from a trust without consideration and a deed upon death under NRS 111.109.

The Recorder also keeps lien records, so a document search shows what is recorded against a property. Owners can record a Declaration of Homestead for protection from involuntary liens. If an inherited house needs a death certificate, it comes from vital statistics in the state where the death occurred, not from the county.

sections.h2: Permit and building issues that slow a sale
sections.html:
Unpermitted work is the item that most often delays a Lyon County sale. The county's building rules cover these basics:

  • A detached shed under 200 square feet with no electrical, mechanical or plumbing needs no permit. Larger sheds, or those with utilities, do.
  • Decks attached to a building need a permit. Detached decks under 200 square feet and less than 30 inches high do not, but must meet code.
  • Fences of seven feet or less need no permit, though front yard fences are limited to 3 feet.
  • A permit lapses if work does not start within 180 days or stops for 180 days.
  • A residential permit's final signed inspection serves as the certificate of occupancy.

Manufactured homes get extra scrutiny. They are allowed in most residential districts when no more than 6 years old at the time of the move, certified under the 1974 federal standard, and at least 1,200 square feet in more than one section. The county warns that unpermitted additions can impair future financing and sale. A failed septic leach field must be replaced under a county permit. In the Mason and Smith valleys, the Walker River Irrigation District must approve site plans. Power is not approved on vacant parcels, which matters when you sell raw land.

Get the exact balance and the dates first, then decide how fast you need to close. At closing, the title company pays unpaid tax out of proceeds. Cash Home Buyers purchases houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to the seller. Confirm every deadline, rate and fee with the Lyon County Assessor, Clerk-Treasurer and Recorder, since official pages change each fiscal year.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in Lyon County, Nevada?
faqs.a: The Clerk-Treasurer collects it, at 27 S Main Street in Yerington or by phone at 775-463-6501. You can also pay online through the county portal, by check or money order mailed to the Lyon County Treasurer, or in the drop box (checks only).

faqs.q: When are Lyon County property tax installments due?
faqs.a: The third Monday of August, then the first Mondays of October, January and March, per NRS 361.483. Each date has a 10-day grace period.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Lyon County property assessment?
faqs.a: January 15, or the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday. File with the Assessor's Office.

faqs.q: Does Lyon County assess property at market value?
faqs.a: No. The Assessor appraises land at market value for its use and buildings at replacement cost new less 1.5% depreciation per year, then takes 35% of that as assessed value. Market value has little bearing on taxable value as buildings age.

faqs.q: Do I owe transfer tax when I sell a house in Lyon County?
faqs.a: Usually yes. The rate is $1.95 per $500 of value, collected by the Recorder when the deed is recorded. Buyer and seller are both responsible, and some transfers are exempt, such as a deed upon death under NRS 111.109.
